interest: Shows Japan's 1939 drought-driven food crisis and the shift to Bern-sourced wartime intelligence on harvests and shipping.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.61317, covering December 22, 1939 to November 24, 1944) documents the escalating rice supply crisis and food administration within Japan and its overseas empire leading into and during World War II. Originating from diplomatic reporting by U.S. Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, analytical memoranda by State Department Far Eastern Affairs specialists, and wartime intelligence gathered by the U.S. Legation in Bern monitoring the German press, the records trace Japan's sudden transition from self-sufficiency to acute grain deficits following the severe summer drought of 1939 in southwestern Japan and southern Korea. Early despatches and internal studies detail the Konoe and Yonai cabinets' emergency interventions—including price ceilings, compulsory requisitioning, the establishment of the Japan Rice Company, milling restrictions, and urban rationing—alongside the severe drain on foreign exchange reserves incurred by emergency rice purchases from Thailand, Burma, and French Indochina. Later wartime intelligence tracks Japan's worsening structural agricultural problems, including severe shortages of fertilizer and rural labor, industrial encroachment on arable land, reliance on substitute crops, the exploitation of occupied territories in Southeast Asia and Manchuria, and State Department evaluations of Japan's vulnerability to an Allied naval blockade.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on the emerging rice crisis in Japan following severe summer droughts in southwestern Japan and southern Korea, detailing government price fixing, distribution controls, and supply calculations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive review of the deteriorating rice supply situation facing the Japanese government at the outset of the 1939–1940 rice year, which observers likened to the conditions preceding the 1918 rice riots. A severe summer drought in southwestern Japan and southern Korea drastically curtailed domestic yields and colonial exports, cutting carry-over stocks by over 50 percent. In response, the Japanese Cabinet enacted price ceilings, established the monopolistic Japan Rice Company, restricted rice polishing to 94 percent, and authorized prefectural governors to requisition grain. Despite these interventions, smallholders and dealers hoarded supplies in anticipation of price increases, forcing the government to plan emergency purchases from abroad despite acute foreign exchange constraints.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4362 from Tokyo Embassy on the Present Rice Problem in Japan

subfiles.about: A reprint of an Oriental Economist article analyzing the rice supply and demand balance sheet following the disastrous drought in Chosen.
subfiles.summary: Oriental Economist article downplays 1939 drought-famine fears in Korea and Japan, proposing rice rationing and imports from colonies to avoid spending on Southeast Asian rice.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 4362: 'Rice Supply Situation' from The Japan Times / The Oriental Economist

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum discussing discrepancies in Japanese rice crop forecasts and the Japanese Diet's decision to suppress grain statistics as military secrets.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Dawson estimates a 10.5-million-koku rice deficit despite revised Japanese forecasts, as the Diet halts publishing crop data, deepening pessimism about the food crisis.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Japanese Rice Production Estimates and Diet Secrecy

subfiles.about: An analytical memorandum by Ivan B. White evaluating Embassy Tokyo's reports on Japan's rice distribution crisis, colonial crop shortfalls, and structural agricultural challenges.
subfiles.summary: White questions Tokyo's optimistic rice-import estimate from Korea given drought and military food demands, warning fertilizer and labor shortages threaten long-term Japanese yields.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum by Ivan B. White Analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 4711

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on mounting domestic rice distribution difficulties, official secrecy, farmer resistance, and the severe foreign exchange drain caused by grain imports.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Japanese government encountered severe obstacles in fulfilling its program to purchase 10.5 million koku of domestic rice for carry-over stocks prior to the 1940 harvest. Intense farmer hoarding, peasant dissatisfaction over input prices, and official secrecy surrounding actual grain reserves provoked widespread public criticism and prompted municipal rationing in smaller centers, with plans to expand rationing to the Kansai region. Grew warns that agricultural productivity is deteriorating due to persistent deficits in commercial fertilizer, farm labor, machinery, and livestock feeds. The despatch underscores that emergency rice purchases from foreign exchange areas severely exceeded the initial estimate of 200 million yen, disrupting international remittances and depriving essential industrial expansion programs of vital capital.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4711 from Tokyo Embassy on Worsening Rice Distribution and Imports

subfiles.about: A comprehensive State Department research memorandum assessing Japan's imperial rice balance, import requirements from Southeast Asia, and vulnerability to an Allied naval blockade.
subfiles.summary: Prepared for Assistant Secretary Henry F. Grady, this extensive study details Japan's shift from domestic self-sufficiency to heavy reliance on external rice imports during the 1939–1940 crop year. Jones estimates that Japan was forced to import approximately 3.5 billion pounds of foreign rice, obtaining 1.5 billion pounds from occupied China and 2.0 billion pounds from Thailand, Burma, and French Indochina. For the 1940–1941 season, domestic Japanese production is projected to contract further due to shortages of fertilizer, labor, and draft animals, but increased colonial shipments and strict state distribution controls are expected to reduce foreign import needs. The memorandum assesses that French Indochina possesses ample exportable surpluses to satisfy Japanese import deficits, and concludes that an Allied naval blockade operating from Hong Kong and Manila would harass shipping but could not decisively sever rice flows or cripple Japan's economy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by J. M. Jones for Assistant Secretary Grady on Japan's Rice Supply

subfiles.about: Minister Harrison transmits German press reports indicating that typhoons reduced the 1942 Japanese rice harvest to 67 million koku.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports Japan's 1942 rice crop fell to 67 million koku on typhoon damage, still near average.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 4920 from Bern Legation on Japanese 1942 Rice Crop

subfiles.about: Minister Harrison reports German press accounts of Japanese Ministry of Agriculture estimates projecting a reduced 1943 rice crop of 62.85 to 63 million koku.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports Japan's 1943 rice estimate fell to about 63 million koku on typhoons, prompting price hikes and crop substitution.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 7773 from Bern Legation on 1943 Japanese Rice Crop Estimates

subfiles.about: Minister Harrison forwards German press reports detailing 1943–1944 crop yields and grain shipments across Japan, Korea, Manchuria, Formosa, and Java.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports flooding cut Japan's rice yields while colonies did better; Formosa ships rice on wooden vessels, and Japan forces Java's population onto corn to free rice for export.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 671 from Bern Legation on Far Eastern Rice and Grain Production

subfiles.about: Minister Harrison reports Japanese occupation plans to forcibly resettle 300,000 residents from Singapore to Malayan provinces to expand rice production.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports Japan is relocating 300,000 Singapore residents to farmland and clearing land in Malaya to cut rice imports.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1150 from Bern Legation on Japanese Rice Self-Sufficiency Plans in Malaya

subfiles.about: Chargé Huddle reports German press releases of Japanese Ministry of Agriculture estimates placing the 1944 rice harvest at 62 million koku amid drought, typhoons, and industrial expansion.
subfiles.summary: Huddle reports Japan's 1944 rice forecast slightly below 1943, hurt by weather and shrinking paddy acreage for industry.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 7747 from Bern Legation on Japanese 1944 Rice Crop and Industrial Land Encroachment
